chapters.title: Chapter One: The Lamp at the End of the Lane

blocks.c: Chapter One: The Lamp at the End of the Lane

The last lamp on Weatherbell Lane had been out for eleven days, and Ines had counted every one of them on the inside of her wrist, in ink, the way her grandmother had taught her to count anything that mattered. Eleven strokes, four of them smudged by rain. The lamp itself stood at the turn where the cobbles gave up and the road became mud with opinions about it.

She had been told, twice, that the lane was not on her round. She had been told once more, with feeling, that a lamp nobody walked under was a lamp nobody needed. Ines had nodded at all three tellings and had come anyway, because the ledger in the guildhall listed the lamp as lit, and Ines had a great and unfashionable respect for ledgers.
The ladder was where she had left it. So was the wind.

At the top of the ladder the world went quiet in the way high places do. The glass housing was clouded with a winter's worth of soot, and inside it the wick sat curled and black, like something asleep and unwilling to discuss the matter.

Ines cleaned the glass first. That was the order: glass, reservoir, wick, flame. Her grandmother had been fond of saying that a lamplighter who lights before she cleans is only making a brighter mess, and had been fonder still of saying it twice.
Light is not a thing you carry to a place. It is a thing a place agrees to keep, if you have asked it properly.

The wick caught on the third strike. It burned yellow, then white, then settled into the steady amber that meant the oil was good and the housing was sealed, and Ines allowed herself, for four full seconds, to be pleased.
Then she looked down the lane and saw that the mud held footprints, and that the footprints had been made by someone walking towards the dark on purpose.

chapters.title: Chapter Two: What the Guild Keeps

blocks.c: Chapter Two: What the Guild Keeps

The guildhall at Weatherbell kept three things: oil, ledgers, and grudges. The oil was in the cellar, the ledgers were on the long shelf, and the grudges were distributed evenly among the staff so that no one person had to carry more than her share.
The Long Shelf

Ines went to the ledgers before she went to anyone who might have an opinion about her going to the ledgers. The relevant volume was bound in grey cloth and smelled of the cellar, and its columns had been ruled by someone with more patience than Ines expected ever to have.
Each lamp in the district had a line. Each line carried four marks:

items: the night it was last lit, in the lighter's own hand
the measure of oil drawn for it
the initials of whoever signed the oil out
a small circle, meaning nothing, which everyone agreed was important

blocks.c: The line for the lamp at the end of the lane was full. Every night accounted for, all eleven of them, in a hand that sloped left and pressed hard enough to emboss the page beneath. Oil drawn each evening. Initials signed each evening. Eleven small circles, drawn carefully, as though by someone who had been told they mattered and had not been told why.
Ines put her thumb on the last entry and found the ink still faintly tacky, which is a thing ink stops being after a day and had no business being after eleven.
"You're touching the book," said the archivist, from the doorway, without heat.
"Someone's been lighting a lamp that isn't lit," said Ines.
The archivist came the rest of the way in and shut the door behind her, which was answer enough for the moment.
Chapter Three: The Counting Song

There is a song lamplighters teach their apprentices, and it is not a good song. It has no tune worth the name and its rhymes are the kind that only work if you are cold and it is late. It exists to be counted along with, one lamp to a line, so that a lighter walking a long round in the dark knows without thinking whether she has missed one.

One for the crossing and two for the well,
three for the door that they never will sell,
four for the corner, and five for the stair,
six for the lamp that was already there.

Ines had learned it at nine and had not thought about the sixth line since. Nobody did. It was the line you sang while fumbling with the ladder, and it meant nothing, and it had always meant nothing, and now she stood in the guildhall cellar with an oil measure in one hand thinking about it with an intensity that frightened her a little.
The archivist's explanation took the better part of an hour and required two cups of the terrible cellar tea.

Some lamps, she said, are lit by the district. Some lamps light the district. The second kind are older than the guild, older than the ledgers, older than the cobbles that gave up at the turn of the lane, and the guild's whole function — its ledgers, its oil, its grudges, its small meaningless circles — was to keep the second kind company so that they did not get bored and wander.
We do not maintain that lamp. We attend it. The distinction is the entire profession, and it is the reason we write everything down.
"And the footprints?" said Ines.
"Ah," said the archivist, and put her cup down. "Those are yours. You simply haven't made them yet."
Chapter Four: Eleven Strokes
She went back at dusk, which is the hour the profession is built around, and she went the long way so she would arrive from the dark end and see the lamp the way the lane saw it.
It was lit. Of course it was lit. She had lit it herself the day before and the oil was good and the housing was sealed, and there was no mystery in a lamp doing exactly what a lamp is for.
The mystery was in the mud, where a fresh set of prints came up the lane towards her, made by boots the size of her own, stopping where she was standing, and going no further.

Ines took the ink pot from her coat. She rolled back her sleeve. Eleven strokes, four of them smudged, and she added a twelfth in the careful, deliberate way you add a thing you intend to be able to point at later.

Above her the wick burned amber and steady and entirely without opinion. Somewhere behind her, at the far end of a round she had not walked yet, another lamp waited to be attended, and the song had a sixth line, and the ledger had a column for all of it.
She picked up the ladder and went to find out what the circles meant.
